case_study_insert.main_stem: Mistral Coffee Roasters (MCR) is a private limited company in the beverage sector, specialising in specialty coffee roasting, employing a workforce of 36. Founded in 2011 by Sofia Mistral, the business supplies independent cafes across the region and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. MCR plans to invest $540,000 in a new automated roasting and packing line, financed by a $320,000 ten-year bank loan and $220,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $189,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.20 a unit and a selling price of $10.50, and produces 80,000 units a year. MCR faces two problems: quality complaints about inconsistent roast colour have risen sharply and absenteeism has reached 7% among packing staff.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report - Q3 2025: MCR roasted 19,500 units of coffee last quarter at a defect rate of 2.4%, down from 3.6% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 44 to 26 a month. Average delivery lead time is 2.8 days. A survey of 500 cafe buyers found 68% would pay up to $0.50 more for certified sustainable beans, and 47% check origin labelling. A skills audit shows 14 of 36 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new roasting controls; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $750 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Mistral Coffee Roasters as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, increasing borrowing costs on MCR's $320,000 variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $12.80 to $13.54 an hour from April 2026. (3) Green coffee bean import prices have risen 9.6% year-on-year, while cafe-sector input inflation is 6.3% and consumer spending on specialty coffee grew 4.1%.

questions.question_text: MCR is funding its $540,000 expansion with a $320,000 bank loan and $220,000 retained profit. Explain two benefits for MCR of using retained profit rather than increasing the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit requires no interest payment and no capital repayment, so using the $220,000 keeps MCR's cash flow free while it services the $320,000 bank loan and meets fixed costs of $189,000 a year. Every dollar of the $540,000 funded internally is a dollar that does not add to the loan commitment, protecting the $10.50 selling price from having to cover extra interest at a time when 7% absenteeism and quality complaints are already disrupting output.

Point 2: Retained profit leaves Sofia Mistral's ownership and control untouched, since no lender can impose conditions on how the new roasting and packing line is run or demand collateral. It is also immediately available and avoids arrangement fees and approval delays, letting MCR respond quickly to cafe demand and to the 68% of 500 surveyed buyers who would pay $0.50 more for certified sustainable beans. Keeping borrowing lower also reduces exposure if rates rise, making the expansion safer for a 36-person roaster.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

questions.question_text: MCR is launching a new single-origin coffee range. Consider cafe trade exhibitions, a social media campaign, or free in-cafe sampling. Which should MCR choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Cafe trade exhibitions: A trade show puts MCR's single-origin range in front of many cafe owners at once and lets buyers taste the product, which helps answer the quality complaints about inconsistent roast colour. It also builds personal contacts with the independent cafes MCR supplies. However, stand fees, travel and staffing are costly for a business funding a $540,000 expansion with a $320,000 loan, and many visitors are competitors or non-buyers, so cost per genuine order can be high.

Social media campaign: A campaign can reach thousands of buyers at low cost per contact and can tell the origin story that 47% of surveyed buyers check. It is measurable and scalable nationally. Its weakness is that coffee is a taste product: an online advert cannot prove roast consistency, and engagement does not reliably convert into cafe orders, especially with a 36-person team and only 19,500 units roasted last quarter.

Free in-cafe sampling: Placing samples in the cafes that already stock MCR lets buyers taste the improvement at the point of purchase, directly tackling the quality complaints. It uses existing distribution, so cost is limited to product giveaway and staff time, and it targets the 68% willing to pay $0.50 more for certified sustainable beans. The drawback is slow reach and reliance on cafe staff.

Recommendation: MCR should choose free in-cafe sampling. It neutralises the quality complaints, uses the existing cafe network instead of costly new channels, and converts the 68% premium preference into trial. Trade exhibitions are rejected as too expensive and untargeted for a 36-employee roaster carrying a $320,000 loan; social media is rejected because it cannot demonstrate taste and is less certain to win cafe orders. MCR can add low-cost social posts later to support the sampling.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited application to MCR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses at least two options with advantages and disadvantages applied to MCR.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of MCR with a justified recommendation and clear rejection of the alternatives.

questions.question_text: MCR's absenteeism has reached 7% and quality complaints about roast colour are rising. Explain two benefits for MCR of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its packing team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 36 employees a voice in how the new roasting and packing line is organised, which helps satisfy social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Workers who help set packing routines are more likely to attend consistently, directly attacking the 7% absenteeism that disrupts the 19,500 units roasted each quarter and the effort to cut the 2.4% defect rate. Because the structure is flat, Sofia Mistral hears these concerns directly.

Point 2: Involving the packing team in decisions generates practical ideas about roast colour and sealing, reducing quality complaints and the 2.4% defect rate. Higher involvement builds commitment and lowers labour turnover, avoiding the $750 per employee cost of off-the-job training replacements and protecting output of 80,000 units while the $540,000 line beds in. Because MCR is flat, democratic suggestions reach Sofia Mistral quickly, so ideas can be acted on without extra management layers, strengthening motivation further and supporting the 68% premium positioning and the certified sustainable launch.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

questions.question_text: MCR must upskill 14 of its 36 staff on the new roasting controls. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should MCR choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training the 14 of 36 staff at the roasting controls is directly relevant to MCR's own machines and quality standards, costs no course fees, and keeps staff productive while they learn, protecting the 19,500 units packed last quarter and the fall in defects to 2.4%. Experienced operators act as trainers, so learning is immediate. Drawbacks are that the trainers' own output suffers, bad habits can spread, and there is no external certificate, which may matter if cafe buyers ask for evidence of competence.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $750 per employee gives structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised certificate for all 14 staff, costing $10,500 in total (14 x $750) - small beside the $540,000 investment. It removes staff from the line, cutting short-term capacity, and generic content may not match MCR's exact roasting settings, so follow-up coaching would still be needed. The college also teaches safety and machine theory that a busy line cannot cover, and a certificate may reassure cafe buyers who audit suppliers. However, releasing 14 of 36 staff at once would remove a large share of the team, so any college course should be staggered across the quarter.

Decision: MCR should choose on-the-job training first, with short college courses later for senior operators. On-the-job training is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids losing output while absenteeism is 7% and quality complaints are already a problem. Full off-the-job training is rejected because paying $10,500 and releasing 14 staff at once would disrupt the 80,000-unit target; the college route can be added once the new line is stable.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to MCR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in the context of MCR.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in the context of MCR with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how MCR's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs / Contribution per unit. Substitution: $189,000 / ($10.50 - $4.20) = $189,000 / $6.30 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price - Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $10.50 - $4.20 = $6.30. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.30.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MCR's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 30,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 80,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 50,000 units, to judge whether to run the new roasting line at full capacity.
2. Contribution per unit of $6.30 allows pricing analysis: if the $0.50 premium researched were won, contribution would rise to $6.80 ($6.30 + $0.50), showing how much volume could be lost before profit falls.
3. Fixed costs of $189,000 and $6.30 contribution set the volume target needed to service the $320,000 bank loan, so managers can check the $540,000 expansion is affordable before committing more capital.
4. Unit cost of $6.56 ($189,000 / 80,000 + $4.20) can be benchmarked each quarter to detect waste and tackle the 2.4% defect rate and the 9.6% rise in green coffee import prices.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.30 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: 50,000-unit margin of safety; pricing with the $0.50 premium; loan-service volume targets; unit-cost benchmarking at $6.56.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MCR's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MCR's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.29 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.49 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.83 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.10 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $95,000 inventories + $140,000 trade receivables + $35,000 cash = $270,000; 2025 current assets = $78,000 + $165,000 + $52,000 = $295,000. Cover of the 2024 current liabilities of $210,000 was $270,000 / $210,000 = 1.29; cover of the 2025 liabilities of $198,000 was $295,000 / $198,000 = 1.49. Liquid assets excluding inventories were $270,000 - $95,000 = $175,000 in 2024, giving $175,000 / $210,000 = 0.83, and $295,000 - $78,000 = $217,000 in 2025, giving $217,000 / $198,000 = 1.10.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened. Cover rose from 1.29 to 1.49, helped by current liabilities falling from $210,000 to $198,000 while current assets rose from $270,000 to $295,000. More importantly, liquid-asset cover improved from 0.83 to 1.10, so MCR no longer depends on selling coffee inventories to meet short-term debts. That matters while it services a $320,000 bank loan and funds a $540,000 expansion. However, trade receivables grew from $140,000 to $165,000, tying up cash; if cafe customers pay late the improvement could reverse. Inventories fell from $95,000 to $78,000, so stock availability for the 80,000-unit target should be watched.

Conclusion: MCR's liquidity has improved. Both cover measures rose and the liquid-asset measure crossed 1.0, so the stronger position does not rest on stock. The residual risk is slower receivable collection, so tighter credit control is advised before further borrowing.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of the current-asset components and a justified conclusion.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MCR of introducing certified sustainable packaging for its coffee range.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Certified sustainable packaging matches the preferences of the 68% of 500 surveyed cafe buyers who would pay up to $0.50 more and the 47% who check origin labelling. That supports MCR's $10.50 selling price and protects the $6.30 contribution per unit, helping absorb the 9.6% rise in green coffee import prices. It also strengthens the brand with independent cafes and supports the single-origin launch, which is important when the new $540,000 roasting line must win enough orders to justify its capacity.

Disadvantage: Certified materials normally cost more than standard bags, so the $4.20 variable cost per unit could rise and squeeze contribution unless the full $0.50 premium is accepted by buyers. Any supply delay or printing error with the new packaging would also push up the 2.4% defect rate and add to the quality complaints already reported. With absenteeism at 7%, staff may struggle to handle a second packaging change while the automated line is still bedding in, risking the 80,000-unit target.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.6% rise in green coffee bean import prices will affect MCR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): The increase is 0.75 percentage points. If MCR's $320,000 loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.75% x $320,000 = $2,400, small against fixed costs of $189,000 and the $540,000 expansion. If the loan is fixed-rate the immediate cost is zero. Higher rates could make cafes cautious and raise the cost of future borrowing, but MCR can cap this by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.54): MCR has a workforce of 36, but the insert gives no hours worked and no individual pay rates, so no annual wage bill can be invented. The defensible benchmark is productivity: 80,000 units / 36 staff = about 2,222 units per worker. If output per worker holds, the rise is absorbable within the $4.20 variable cost and $6.30 contribution; if 7% absenteeism reduces output, unit labour cost rises. It is a recurring, unavoidable cost but cannot be quantified from the insert.

Input cost inflation (9.6% green coffee): The insert does not decompose the $4.20 variable cost, so only a labelled upper bound is honest: if the whole $4.20 rose 9.6%, that is 9.6% x $4.20 = about $0.40 per unit, or roughly $32,000 a year at 80,000 units. That directly erodes the $6.30 contribution that justifies the $540,000 line. MCR can recover part through the $0.50 premium accepted by 68% of buyers.

Conclusion: The 9.6% rise in green coffee import prices will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every unit sold and hits contribution directly, unlike the one-off $2,400 interest effect; the wage rise matters but is unquantifiable and partly offset by productivity, whereas ingredient costs strike at the margin that funds the expansion.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on MCR's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of MCR with a well-justified judgement on the greatest impact.
